# AI Novelty & Feasibility Audit
## Project: Benchmarking Vision Encoder Quantization Sensitivity in Driving VLMs on Edge Hardware

**Audit generated by:** Claude (Anthropic) — claude-opus-4-6
**Date:** September 2026
**Team:** Yiang (Aeon) Shen, Maximilian (Max) Garcia
**Course:** CMPE 249 — Intelligent Autonomous Systems (Fall 2026)

---

## 1. Project Summary

This project benchmarks how aggressively the vision encoder in modern driving Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can be quantized before driving-task performance degrades, measured on a physical NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB. The core finding motivating this work — that vision encoders are significantly more sensitive to quantization than language decoders — has been established in general-domain VLM research (MBQ, CVPR 2025; Shin et al., ICML 2026 Workshop) but never characterized on driving benchmarks, at aggressive precision levels (INT4/FP4), or on the Orin Nano specifically.

We apply component-wise quantization (vision encoder and language decoder quantized independently at FP16 / INT8 / INT4) to Qwen3 VL 4B, run inference on the DriveLM-nuScenes graph VQA benchmark, and score outputs offline using an LLM-as-judge. The contribution is the sensitivity characterization itself — actionable thresholds for edge deployment — not beating any SOTA.

## 2. Red Ocean Analysis — Oversaturated Areas We Avoided

### ❌ Standard Object Detection Quantization (v1 — rejected)
- INT8 quantization of YOLO-family models on Jetson hardware is exhaustively documented by NVIDIA, Ultralytics, and open-source tutorials.
- Prof. Liu rejected this direction explicitly: "too old, companies already do this."
- Reporting mAP before/after quantization alone is an engineering exercise, not a research contribution.

### ❌ BEV Fusion & Multi-Sensor Pipelines
- BEVFusion, BEVFormer, and sensor-fusion architectures dominate CVPR/NeurIPS submissions (2022–2025). Every major AV company publishes in this space. Academic differentiation is nearly impossible at the MS project level.

### ❌ End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Generative Models
- Cosmos/World Foundation Models for autonomous driving are heavily pursued by NVIDIA Research with compute budgets no academic team can match. (An early misunderstanding attributed a Cosmos suggestion to Prof. Liu; this was traced to a teammate's misinterpretation of a class comment and explicitly dropped.)

### ❌ Uniform VLM Quantization Benchmarking
- Applying the same precision level to an entire VLM and reporting average accuracy is already covered by standard quantization toolchains (TensorRT, llama.cpp). The interesting question is *which components* tolerate quantization and which don't — uniform benchmarking misses this entirely.

## 3. Prior Work Threat Assessment

Two papers require prominent citation and careful positioning because they overlap with our experimental shape:

### 🔴 MBQ — Modality-Balanced Quantization (CVPR 2025)
- **Overlap:** Established the vision-vs-language quantization sensitivity asymmetry as their core finding. They propose a mixed-precision scheme that assigns higher precision to vision-sensitive layers.
- **Gap we fill:** MBQ evaluates on general-domain VLM benchmarks (MMBench, TextVQA, ScienceQA) — never on driving tasks. They test on datacenter GPUs — never on edge hardware. Their models are 7B+ — never sub-5B.
- **Reframing:** We don't claim to *discover* the asymmetry. We *characterize* it in the driving domain, at precision levels and model scales MBQ didn't cover, on hardware they didn't deploy to.

### 🔴 Shin et al. — Rethinking Small VLM Quantization (ICML 2026 Workshop)
- **Overlap:** Component-wise VLM quantization ablations (vision encoder / projector / LLM decoder quantized independently) on Jetson Orin hardware with sub-3B VLMs. This is our exact experimental shape.
- **Gaps we fill (four distinct ones):**
  1. **Vision encoder precision floor:** Shin et al. never push vision encoder quantization below INT8. We test INT4/FP4.
  2. **Task domain:** They evaluate on MME (general-domain). We evaluate on DriveLM (driving-specific graph VQA).
  3. **Hardware tier:** They use Jetson Orin NX and AGX Orin. They explicitly excluded the Orin Nano — their Appendix notes that sub-3B VLMs OOM'd on it with BitsAndBytes. We target the Nano specifically.
  4. **Quantization backend:** They use BitsAndBytes (which their own appendix flags as having anomalous overhead compared to AWQ). We use TensorRT-LLM / GGUF.
- **Reframing:** We extend Shin et al.'s component-wise framework into precision regimes, task domains, and hardware tiers they did not cover.

### 🟡 Supporting Evidence (not threats)
- **ReasonDrive, VTS, MPDrive** all freeze vision encoder weights during fine-tuning while adapting language layers — treating the vision encoder as the more fragile component. This is indirect but consistent evidence supporting the asymmetry hypothesis.
- **RegCache** (prefix register caching) provides structural evidence that vision encoder quantization is architecturally harder than decoder quantization.
- **Bi-VLM** (2-bit ultra-low PTQ) operates in a different regime entirely. One useful finding: 90–99% of image tokens are redundant post-quantization.

## 4. Blue Ocean Analysis — Genuine Novelty

### ✅ Core Novel Contribution

**No existing paper combines all three:** component-wise VLM quantization analysis + driving-specific benchmark (DriveLM) + actual edge hardware deployment (Jetson Orin Nano).

This is the project's Related Work table in one sentence: DriveLM papers don't quantize, quantization papers don't test driving tasks, and neither deploys on edge hardware. We sit at the intersection.

### ✅ Novel Dimensions (each individually extends prior work)

**1. Aggressive vision encoder precision on driving tasks**
- Pushing vision encoder to INT4/FP4 on DriveLM has never been done. Shin et al. stopped at INT8.
- The question "does INT4 vision encoding destroy spatial reasoning needed for driving but preserve object recognition?" has no answer in the literature.

**2. Task-type sensitivity breakdown**
- DriveLM categorizes questions into perception / prediction / planning / behavior. ReasonDrive shows these have different difficulty profiles (perception: 0.68, planning: harder). We test whether quantization sensitivity follows the same pattern or reveals different ordering — e.g., perception may be more vision-sensitive while planning relies more on language reasoning.

**3. Orin Nano deployment (memory-constrained edge)**
- Shin et al.'s own paper documents why the Orin Nano was excluded: OOM with BitsAndBytes. We specifically target this hardware gap, using TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA's own stack for Jetson) instead.

**4. Direct downstream extension of Prof. Liu's MoRAL**
- Prof. Liu's MoRAL paper (IEEE IMC 2026) deploys a compact driving VLM on nuScenes with an LLM-as-judge evaluation pipeline. His Future Work section explicitly calls for quantization characterization on edge hardware. Our project maps directly onto this gap.

Appropriate for an MS course project; borderline for a workshop paper depending on result strength.

## 6. Feasibility Assessment

### Hardware Feasibility
- Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB physically in hand (borrowed from Prof. Liu's lab).
- ~6 GB usable GPU memory after OS overhead. Qwen3 VL 4B at FP16 is tight (~8 GB) — may need to start at INT8 baseline or use a smaller model as fallback.
- No hardware-sharing risk: device stays with Aeon in San Jose for the full semester.

### Toolchain Feasibility
- **TensorRT-LLM** (primary): NVIDIA's own stack, designed for Jetson. Supports INT8 and INT4/FP4. Per-component quantization (vision encoder vs. decoder independently) is the key open question — needs validation from Max.
- **llama.cpp / GGUF** (fallback): Broader model support, fine-grained layer-group quantization via GGUF format. If TensorRT-LLM doesn't support Qwen3 VL cleanly, this path is available.
- **Neither team member has TensorRT-LLM experience.** Timeline explicitly includes 2–3 weeks of ramp-up. This is honest, not a weakness — the learning is part of the project scope.

### Evaluation Feasibility
- DriveLM-nuScenes is public with established eval protocol (GPT Score via LLM-as-judge).
- Evaluation splits into on-device (inference + logging) and offline (judge model scoring on laptop/cloud). The Jetson doesn't need to run the judge.
- LLM-as-judge targeting Gemma 4 31B — runs on a separate machine. Fallback: AutoDrive-QA MCQ format (Khalili & Smyth, 2025), which converts DriveLM into multiple-choice with zero-cost scoring.

### Timeline Feasibility
- 11-week timeline with explicit ramp-up acknowledgment in weeks 1–3.
- Risk-adjusted: if TensorRT-LLM doesn't work, GGUF fallback avoids full restart.
- Minimum viable result: sensitivity curves for a single model at 3 precision levels on a DriveLM subset. This is achievable even with delays.

### Risk Table

| Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3 VL 4B doesn't fit on Jetson at FP16 | Medium | Start at INT8 baseline; fall back to smaller model |
| TensorRT-LLM doesn't support Qwen3 VL | Medium | Switch to llama.cpp/GGUF |
| Per-component quantization not possible in toolchain | Low | Report uniform quantization results; note limitation |
| DriveLM eval too large for full Jetson inference | Low | Use representative subset (500 frames) |
| GPT Score eval too costly or unreliable | Low | Fall back to AutoDrive-QA MCQ format |
| Second model unavailable | Low | Depth over breadth on primary model |

## 7. AI Critique — Honest Limitations

- **Novelty ceiling:** The vision encoder sensitivity finding is already published (MBQ, Shin et al.). Our contribution is empirical characterization in a new regime, not a new discovery. This is appropriate for a course project but should be framed carefully to avoid overclaiming.
- **Single-model risk:** If results come only from Qwen3 VL 4B, generalizability claims are limited. A second model with a different vision encoder architecture would strengthen the work, but is not guaranteed.
- **Toolchain uncertainty:** The TensorRT-LLM learning curve is real. If component-wise quantization turns out to be non-trivial to set up, the core experimental matrix may take longer than planned.
- **Benchmark scope:** DriveLM uses still-frame graph VQA — it doesn't capture temporal reasoning. Results may not generalize to video-based driving tasks (though this is a scope limitation, not a flaw — we chose DriveLM deliberately because video VQA requires 42+ GB memory).
- **Zero-shot vs. fine-tuned:** Our baselines (Qwen3 VL 4B zero-shot on DriveLM) may underperform published fine-tuned baselines (ReasonDrive's Qwen2.5-VL achieves 0.45–0.54 with reasoning chains). The comparison is still valid for measuring relative degradation across precision levels, but absolute scores will be lower.

---

## 8. Conclusion

This project occupies a genuine gap at the intersection of VLM quantization, driving-task evaluation, and edge hardware deployment. The direction was confirmed through Prof. Liu's in-person guidance, aligns directly with his own published research agenda (MoRAL Future Work), and is positioned carefully against the two closest prior works (MBQ and Shin et al.).

The core framing principle: **we are not discovering the vision encoder sensitivity phenomenon — we are characterizing it in a regime where no one else has looked.** All scope decisions (model, benchmark, hardware, toolchain) should protect this characterization contribution.

**Key risks are managed, not eliminated.** The TensorRT-LLM ramp-up and per-component quantization support are the biggest unknowns. The GGUF fallback ensures the project doesn't collapse if the primary toolchain fails.
